extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, newsroom editors, and academic publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended practices for science journalists and newsrooms on detecting, reporting, and updating stories when scientific papers are retracted, and on publisher/aggregator responsibilities to signal retraction status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat retractions as continuation of the news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating a retraction as a “continuation of the news story” — providing plain language updates that explain how the original claims have changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides plain-language updates to bridge the gap between scientific correction and public understanding; requires journalists to write new stories when retraction occurs. Anti-pattern: ignoring retractions and letting misleading information persist in the public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated monitoring tools for retraction status
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong desire among journalists for automated tools that can monitor the retraction status of papers previously cited in news articles and alert reporters of any 'expressions of concern' or removals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tools should proactively notify reporters about changes; journalists currently rely on luck, social media, or informal networks to discover retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers proactively notify previously relevant readers and reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should adopt systems to automatically and proactively notify journalists, registered users, and researchers who previously accessed or downloaded a specific article when it is retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic, targeted notifications can reduce reliance on chance discovery. This includes notifying journalists who cited the work and users who downloaded it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust DOI resolution integrating article, retraction, and republication
rubrics_metrics.description: A robust DOI resolution system that integrates the original paper, retraction notice, and any republication into a single, inseparable set for the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Would help ensure users encountering the record see the full history; current problem: retractions often marked on publisher platforms but not consistently across aggregators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear retraction watermark on full text
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should not make the full text of retracted articles freely available without a clear 'RETRACTED' watermark on every page to prevent misunderstanding about a paper's status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent readers from inadvertently treating retracted content as current. The article notes some of these practices already exist 'on the edges' but recommends broader adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure retraction status propagation across aggregators and libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction markings must be reflected not just on publisher sites but also on content aggregators (e.g., PubMed) and personalized libraries (e.g., Mendeley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A major problem is inconsistent signage across platforms; remedy requires coordination so retraction metadata follows the article record everywhere users access it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal uncertainty in initial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Signalling uncertainty with phrases like 'early results suggest' can maintain reader trust if findings are later disconfirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using cautious language in first reports frames findings as provisional. This is a practical tactic journalists described to preserve credibility when corrections occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build protected verification time and editorial support
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms could build in protected verification time and strengthen editorial support systems to safeguard accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses structural/resource barriers (e.g., 15-minute verification windows); anti-patterns include pressure to 'move to the next hot topic' and insufficient time allocated for retrospective checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate and resource retrospective verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that checking for retractions is often uncompensated work, particularly for freelance writers; ensure time and pay are provided for retrospective verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic models (payment-per-story) discourage follow-ups; remedy includes allocating paid time or editorial resources for updates and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and enforce a code of conduct requiring updates and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: A code of conduct for journalism and newsrooms should be explicit and strictly enforce the principle to gather, update and correct information throughout the life of a news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Would institutionalize responsibility for follow-ups and corrections; enforcement mechanisms and editorial policies should be specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid framing retractions as evidence of systemic corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid news stories that turn examples of successful detection and correction into suggestions of widespread corruption and conspiracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: focusing on individual fraud narratives to attract engagement, which reframes retractions as contested authority rather than normal scientific self-correction. Instead, contextualize retractions as part of normal correction processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on systemic and procedural causes, not only individual misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage more deeply with the procedural and structural aspects of retraction (e.g., fake peer review, procedural errors, 'publish or perish' incentives) rather than privileging individual misconduct stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative reporting into institutional practices can illuminate root causes and improve public understanding; relying on human-interest fraud narratives obscures systemic vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use retraction coverage to highlight scientific self-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting retractions as evidence of effective self-correction in science can boost institutional credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing matters: presenting retractions as corrective processes can increase trust rather than erode it, if explained clearly to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentivize journalists who publish follow-ups and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and reward journalists who prioritize transparency by publishing follow-up pieces that state 'We were wrong, and here’s what changed' (e.g., a Ctrl-Z Award for journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards or incentives could change norms by valuing correction work; the example suggests celebrating transparency and correction as journalistic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic institutions should support development of monitoring tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic institutions should support the development of tools to help journalists monitor the scientific record more efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journalists expressed enthusiasm for such tools; institutional support (technical and funding) can help build the systems reporters need.
